newsitem.title: USA: New York mayor demands removal of U.N. envoys.
newsitem.headline: New York mayor demands removal of U.N. envoys.

text.p: Mayor Rudolph Giuliani wrote letters on Thursday to the ambassadors of Russia and Belarus demanding that two diplomats charged in a punchup with New York City police officers be recalled from their posts.

Police officials said two officers pulled the Russian from his car on Sunday because he appeared intoxicated and refused to show his driver's license after being ticketed for illegal parking near a fire hydrant. They said the Belarus diplomat then jumped out and punched one of the policemen.
"Of course we're not going to apologise," Giuliani told reporters. "I'm very proud of what the police officers did, they did their job trying to stop drunk people from driving.

"Send them back to where they came from ... they're not welcome here," said Giuliani, a former prosecutor who has won acclaim for fighting crime in New York City since he became mayor three years ago.

Russia said police had beaten and arrested one of its diplomats in New York and demanded an apology from Washington. The State Department said it was awaiting an investigation by New York City police.
The charges against the envoys, both attached to U.N. missions, were dropped on Sunday after they claimed diplomatic immunity.
Giuliani told reporters it "should not go without notice" that during the first six months of last year, 122 vehicles registered with the Russian mission received 14,437 summonses for violations.
He said in his letter to the ambassodor of Belarus that in the first six months of 1996, 15 vehicles from the mission had received 828 summonses.
Diplomats and other employees of foreign embassies in the United States are obligated to abide by U.S. law but under the 1961 Treaty of Vienna they have diplomatic immunity from prosecution.
U.S. officials said if a diplomat committed a minor offence, the infraction was usually played down and the incident ended there.
But in the case of a serious offence, like a felony, the State Department asks the foreign government involved to waive immunity so the diplomat can be tried in U.S. courts.

If the foreign government refuses, and Washington believes there is probable cause the diplomat is guilty of the offence, then the United States asks the diplomat to leave the country and is barred from re-entering the country.
